content: Countries are encouraged to implement national regulatory changes to permit the cost-effective intradermal administration of rabies vaccines. Cell-culture-based rabies vaccines (CCEEVs) are generally safe and well-tolerated. However, adverse events may occur, influenced partly by the purity of the inactivated rabies virus (RABV), which can vary between batches. Minor, transient reactions such as erythema, pain, or swelling at the injection site occur in 35–45% of vaccinated individuals, particularly after intradermal booster administration. Mild systemic adverse events, including transient fever, headache, dizziness, and gastrointestinal symptoms, are observed in 5–15% of cases. Serious adverse events, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and allergic reactions, are rare. True vaccine failures are exceedingly rare when high-quality CCEEVs are used alongside proper wound care, adherence to the cold chain, and compliance with vaccination schedules. However, factors such as poor vaccine quality or improper cold chain maintenance can contribute to treatment failure and subsequent death. CCEEVs establish immunological memory that is believed to persist for the individual’s lifetime, even when neutralizing antibody titers decrease or become undetectable. Clinical data confirm that vaccinated individuals respond to booster immunization within seven days, even decades after the initial vaccination course, regardless of the route of administration or the presence of detectable RABV-specific antibodies at the time of the booster. Failures of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), where patients die despite receiving the correct protocol in a timely manner, are extremely rare among the estimated 20 million people who receive PEP annually. Reported PEP failures have occurred primarily in developing countries and often involve deviations from WHO-recommended protocols, such as failure to inject all bite sites, inadequate wound care, or the use of poor-quality rabies vaccines. Passive immunization products available include human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG), equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG), and highly purified F(ab')2 fragments derived from equine immunoglobulin. Patients with open wounds from suspected or confirmed rabid animals should receive passive immunization as specified in WHO guidelines. Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) should be administered with the first vaccine dose, directly into and around the wound site. Proper wound cleaning, deep irrigation, and the application of a potent antiseptic agent, along with timely administration of the first CCEEV dose, are critical for survival when RIG is unavailable. HRIG should be given at a maximum dose of 20 IU/kg of body weight, while ERIG should be administered at 40 IU/kg. ERIG is significantly less expensive than HRIG, and newer equine preparations are potent, highly purified, and safe, with minimal adverse events. Serum sickness may occur in less than 1–3% of recipients of highly purified ERIG, typically one week after administration. The risk of anaphylactic reactions is low (1 in 150,000) and generally treatable. Skin tests are not recommended before ERIG administration, as they poorly predict severe adverse events and should not deter the use of ERIG when needed. ERIG should be administered under conditions that allow for the management of anaphylactic reactions. RIGs are in short supply globally, and new technologies, such as monoclonal antibody (mAb) cocktails, may serve as alternatives for PEP. WHO has recommended mAb cocktails containing at least two antibodies against RABV as substitutes for RIGs. The first licensed mAb, produced by the Serum Institute of India, has shown equivalent performance to HRIG in studies and could address critical public health gaps. Vaccination before or after exposure to rabies is nearly 100% effective in preventing the disease when combined with proper wound care and RIG administration, if indicated. Vaccines can be administered intradermally or intramuscularly. Intramuscular vaccines can be safely used intradermally, even if this constitutes off-label use. For intradermal administration, recommended sites include the deltoids, lateral thighs, or suprascapular areas. For intramuscular administration, the deltoid muscle is recommended for adults and children aged ≥2 years, while the anterolateral thigh is preferred for children aged <2 years. Vaccines should not be administered in the gluteal area due to unreliable immune response induction. Vaccination schedules should be completed within the stipulated time, but restarting the series is unnecessary if doses are delayed by a few days. Rabies vaccines and RIG can be used during pregnancy and lactation. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is strongly recommended for individuals at high risk of exposure to RABV or other lyssaviruses due to their occupation, activities, or residence in remote or endemic areas. PrEP eliminates the need for RIG administration after a bite and induces immunological memory that likely lasts a lifetime if PEP is administered after exposure. Intradermal PrEP should be administered to enough individuals in the same session to ensure opened vials are used within 6–8 hours. Single-day priming vaccination may be considered for healthy individuals aged 5–47 years when time constraints prevent a two-visit PrEP schedule. However, there is no evidence that single-day priming induces long-term immunity (>1 year).
